rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
The Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) before the birth covers the last six weeks before the delivery. During that time your employer may not employ you unless you expressly declare that you are willing to work, and you can withdraw that declaration at any time for the future.

The period is counted from the expected day of delivery shown on a doctor's or midwife's certificate. If 15 November 2026 is the date on that certificate, the six weeks are counted back from that date, which places the start in early October 2026. Your employer and your health insurance fund work from the date on the certificate.

If the baby does not arrive on the expected day, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match. If the baby comes early, the time lost before the birth is added to the period after the birth.

After the birth, your employer may not employ you until eight weeks have passed. This extends to twelve weeks for premature births, multiple births, or if a disability in the child is medically confirmed within eight weeks. In that last case it only applies if you request it.

Tell your employer about the pregnancy and the expected date as soon as you know. If your employer asks, provide a certificate from a doctor or midwife showing the expected date.

These rules are in the maternity protection law. That law does not cover self-employed people.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set a cut-off date for applying. It limits how far back payment reaches. Elterngeld (parental allowance) must be applied for in writing. It is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the start of the month of the child's life in which your application was received. Months of the child's life before that are not paid. These are counted in the child's months of life, starting from the birth, not calendar months.

Elterngeld can be drawn from the day of birth. Applications received later than this backdating window allows lose those earlier months of payment.

The same three-month limit applies if you later change the months you chose in your application. Changes are also generally not allowed for months already paid out, except in cases of particular hardship.

Applications and changes go to the Elterngeld office responsible for you. That office decides how the rule applies to your application.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
For Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)), the law sets two notice periods. You must request it from your employer in text form:

- at least seven weeks before it starts, for leave up to your child's third birthday
- at least 13 weeks before it starts, for leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year

When you request Elternzeit for the period up to the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take. If a mother takes Elternzeit straight after her maternity protection period, that period counts toward these two years.

In urgent cases, a shorter reasonable notice period is possible as an exception. The official family portal gives premature birth as an example and says the period then depends on the individual case.

If a mother cannot request Elternzeit in time, for a reason that is not her fault, for leave starting directly after her maternity protection period, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends.

Text form means a letter without a signature or an email is enough. Your employer must confirm your Elternzeit to you.

These notice rules are taken from the current statute. The excerpts here do not show whether an earlier rule applies to children born some years ago.

Elternzeit is arranged with your employer, not applied for at an authority.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Under Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period), an employer may not employ a woman until eight weeks after the birth. If the baby comes early, two separate rules can lengthen this.

1. Any early birth: the protection period before the birth is normally six weeks before the expected due date. If the baby arrives before that date, the time before the birth is shorter. The period after the birth is extended by the same number of days. The official family portal describes this as the total period staying at 14 weeks, ending a few days later than eight weeks after the birth.

2. Premature births: for premature births, the period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks instead of eight. The extension for an early delivery described above is added on top of these twelve weeks. The law does not define "premature" in this section. The family portal gives an example: a baby weighing less than 2,500 grams at birth. It describes the total Mutterschutz in this case as rising from 14 to 18 weeks.

The period after the birth cannot be waived. Unlike the period before the birth, you may not choose to work during it. The exception is school and university students, who may resume their studies if they expressly ask to.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. During your pregnancy your employer is not allowed to dismiss you. This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) lasts from the start of the pregnancy until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth. The same protection applies for four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy.

The protection applies if your employer knows about the pregnancy when giving notice. It also applies if you tell your employer within two weeks of receiving the notice. Missing those two weeks does no harm if it was not your fault and you tell your employer without delay. The official guidance adds that the protection applies even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, as long as you were already pregnant when you received the notice.

There are exceptions, but only in special cases that are not connected to the pregnancy, a miscarriage or the birth. Only the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can declare a dismissal permissible in such a case. The dismissal must then be in writing and must state the reason. The official guidance gives examples such as the company's insolvency, a partial closure of the business, or a very serious breach of duty. Without the authority's approval, the dismissal is invalid.

If you are dismissed without that approval, the official guidance says you must file a claim at the labour court. The claim must normally be filed within 3 weeks of receiving the written notice. If you do not file a claim, the dismissal is treated as valid. You can file it yourself, through a lawyer, or orally at the court office. The guidance also recommends contacting the supervisory authority.

If the authority approved the dismissal, you can challenge that approval. Depending on the federal state, this is done by an objection or by a lawsuit. This is a separate procedure. It does not replace the claim at the labour court.

If you take parental leave after the birth, a separate protection against dismissal can apply. It covers the period from when the leave was requested, within set limits, and the leave itself.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under federal law, the right to Elterngeld (parental allowance) ends above a set level of zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income).

What the statute says for the current rule:
- A person has no claim if their zu versteuerndes Einkommen in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros.
- If another person also meets the conditions, for example the other parent, the claim ends if the two incomes together are more than 175,000 euros.

Zu versteuerndes Einkommen is not the same as gross income. The official family portal explains that it is usually much lower than gross pay, because deductions and allowances are subtracted first. The figure is set by the tax office and appears on your tax assessment notice.

If the tax assessment for the year before the birth is not yet available, you can still apply. In that case the law provides for a provisional decision. If the application indicates the limit is likely not exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation. It can be withdrawn if the limit turns out to have been exceeded.

Earlier births: the official family portal describes different, higher limits for children born before the current rule took effect. The excerpts available here do not include the statute's transitional provision, so this answer does not say which limit applies to a particular birth date.

Whether your family is above or below the limit, and which rule applies to your child's birth, is decided only by the Elterngeld office responsible for your application.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The law sets the totals as follows. It does not fix one number for every family. It depends on which variant you choose, how you split the months, and whether certain conditions are met.

Elterngeld (parental allowance) comes in a basic variant and a Plus variant.

- Parents together are entitled to 12 basic monthly amounts.
- They are entitled to 2 further basic months (called partner months) if one parent's income from work is reduced in two months of the child's life.
- One parent can receive at most 12 basic monthly amounts, plus at most 4 monthly amounts of partnership bonus.
- Instead of one basic month, a parent can take two months of the Plus variant. The Plus variant therefore lasts twice as long.
- Each parent who receives Elterngeld must take it for at least two months of the child's life.

The official family portal explains that the partnership bonus is for parents who both work part-time at the same time. It also explains that single parents can receive the partner months and the partnership bonus.

There are also time limits on when the months can be used:

- The basic variant can be received until the child completes its 14th month of life.
- The Plus variant can be received until the child completes its 32nd month of life. From the 15th month onward, at least one parent must take it in consecutive months.
- Both parents can receive the basic variant at the same time in only one of the first 12 months of life. This limit does not apply to multiple births, premature births, children with a medically confirmed disability, and some sibling cases.
- The months are paid per month of the child's life, not per calendar month.

For premature births, the joint basic entitlement is higher:

- 13 months if the child was born at least 6 weeks before the expected delivery date
- 14 months if born at least 8 weeks early
- 15 months if born at least 12 weeks early
- 16 months if born at least 16 weeks early

The expected date in the doctor's or midwife's certificate is what counts.

How many months your family will actually receive is decided by the responsible Elterngeld authority when it assesses your application. In the application you state which months you claim in which variant.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is a set of extra parental allowance months for parents who both work part-time at the same time.

What the law says:
- If both parents work no fewer than 24 and no more than 32 hours a week, averaged over a month of the child's life, and both meet the general entitlement conditions in section 1 of the same law, each parent gets an additional monthly payment for that month. The payment is of the lower-rate, longer-running form of parental allowance (BEEG §4b(1)).
- Each parent can receive at most four Partnerschaftsbonus payments. It can only be received for at least two months (BEEG §4b(2)).
- Both parents must take it at the same time, in consecutive months of the child's life (BEEG §4b(3)).
- If it later turns out that the conditions were not met in every month applied for, the consecutive-months requirement still counts as met (BEEG §4b(5)).

Single parents:
- One parent can receive these extra months alone in three situations. The first is that the parent meets the conditions for the income-tax relief for single parents and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child. The second is that care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare. The third is that care by the other parent is impossible, for example because of serious illness or severe disability. That parent must work 24 to 32 hours a week on average in two to four consecutive months (BEEG §4c(1) and (2)).
- If one of these situations arises while both parents are already receiving the Partnerschaftsbonus, one parent can continue receiving it alone (BEEG §4b(4)).

What the official guidance adds:
- The Partnerschaftsbonus is calculated in the same way as the lower-rate form of parental allowance. Depending on income before the birth, it is between 150 and 900 euros a month per parent.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
In statutory health insurance, a baby is usually covered through Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants). The law says the children of members of a statutory health insurance fund are insured if the child:

- lives or usually stays in Germany,
- is not insured in their own right or voluntarily,
- is not exempt from compulsory insurance,
- is not mainly self-employed, and
- has no regular total income above a set limit.

Children are covered under these rules until they turn 18.

There is one exception that matters for many families. A child is not covered through Familienversicherung if the parent related to the child is the member's spouse or civil partner, that parent is not a member of a statutory health insurance fund, and that parent's total income regularly exceeds one-twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling (Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze) and is regularly higher than the member's income.

In practice, the steps start with registering the birth. The registry office responsible for the place of birth must be notified within one week. It issues the birth certificate. You need the birth certificate to register the child with the health insurance fund.

Whether your baby is covered through Familienversicherung is decided by your statutory health insurance fund, not by this service. These excerpts do not cover private health insurance. If one parent is privately insured, ask the private insurer and the statutory fund how the child can be insured.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
What it is: Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of birth itself. The protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the expected birth date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

Who pays depends on your health insurance:
- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld from that insurer under the rules of the Social Code, Book V (MuSchG §19(1)).
- If you are employed when the protection period before the birth begins, the payment is your average daily net pay from the last three settled calendar months, up to 13 euros per calendar day. If your pay was higher, your employer pays the difference as a supplement (SGB V §24i(2), MuSchG §20(1)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, the federal government pays Mutterschaftsgeld, up to 210 euros in total. It is paid on application by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

When to apply: the excerpts I have do not give an application date or time limit for the health insurer's payment. They do say that payment before the birth is based on a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected date of birth (SGB V §24i(3)). For exact timing and the forms, ask your statutory health insurer, or the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung if you are not statutorily insured.

Whether you qualify and how much you receive is decided by your health insurer or, if you are not statutorily insured, by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, being in a relationship with the mother is not enough. The law names three ways a man becomes a child's legal father: he is married to the mother at the time of the birth, he has acknowledged paternity, or a court has established his paternity (BGB §1592).

If you are not married when the child is born, your partner must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count legally as the father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent. The acknowledgement can already be made before the birth (BGB §1594(4)). It cannot be made subject to a condition or a time limit (BGB §1594(3)).

The father must make his declaration in person at a competent office, for example the youth welfare office, a civil registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the federal state, it may cost a fee at a notary or local court.

A Vaterschaftsanerkennung is not effective while another man's paternity exists (BGB §1594(2)). For example, if the mother is married to another man at the time of the birth, her husband is the legal father, and an acknowledgement cannot be made except in the divorce situation the official guidance describes.

Legal fatherhood does not automatically give the father parental custody. For unmarried parents, the mother has custody from the birth. For joint custody, both parents must also declare that they want joint custody, or a family court must decide. Marrying after the birth also creates joint custody. The youth welfare office advises on custody questions.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody on her own. Under federal law, unmarried parents get joint custody in one of three ways:

1. Both parents declare that they want to take on custody together. This is called a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody).
2. The parents marry each other.
3. The family court transfers joint custody to both parents.

If none of these happens, the mother keeps sole custody.

Before the father can share custody, he must be the legal father. That happens when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give the father custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Whether your baby will be German is a decision about your family, so I cannot give you a yes or no. Here is the general rule.

German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) is acquired at birth in two main ways under federal law:

1. By descent: a child becomes German at birth if one parent holds German Staatsangehörigkeit.

2. By birth in Germany to foreign parents: a child of foreign parents born in Germany becomes German at birth if one parent meets both of these conditions:
- has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years, and
- holds an unlimited right of residence, or holds a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement as a Swiss citizen or a Swiss citizen's family member.

Only one parent needs to meet both conditions. When the child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit this way, it is entered in the birth register where the birth is recorded.

If a child born in Germany does not become German, a separate rule covers residence. If both parents hold a residence permit, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit at the time of birth, the child is granted a residence permit automatically. If only one parent holds one of these, the child may be granted one. If a parent holds a visa or may stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

Whether your family meets these conditions is decided by the authorities when the birth is registered, not by this product. These excerpts do not cover whether your child also acquires Indian citizenship. The Indian embassy or consulate responsible for your area handles that question.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
Whether a child born in Germany needs an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) depends on the parents' status at the time of birth. The law sets out these rules.

Children of German parents: a child acquires German citizenship by birth if one parent is a German citizen (StAG §4(1)). Extra conditions apply if only the father is German and paternity has to be acknowledged or established.

Children of foreign parents who acquire German citizenship: a child born in Germany to foreign parents acquires German citizenship by birth if one parent has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years and holds an unlimited right of residence. A parent who is a Swiss citizen or a family member of one may instead hold a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement (StAG §4(3)).

Residence rules for a child born in Germany (AufenthG §33):
- If both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit at the time of birth, the child is granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis automatically by the authorities.
- If only one parent holds one of these permits, the authorities may grant the child an Aufenthaltserlaubnis on their own initiative.
- If a parent holds a visa at the time of birth, or is allowed to stay without a visa, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

Which of these applies to your child depends on your citizenship and permits at the time of birth. The provided sources do not say which office handles this. The decision on your child's status is made by the authority responsible for residence matters where you live, not by this service.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a general rule. Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is offset against Elterngeld (parental allowance). The law lists Mutterschaftsgeld under the Fifth Book of the Social Code and the employer's supplement to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20 as income that is offset against Elterngeld, for the period from the day of the child's birth. Mutterschaftsgeld paid for the time before the birth is not covered by this rule.

One exception: the one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros, paid by the Federal Office for Social Security to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer, is not offset.

How the offset works, according to the official family portal:
- Maternity benefits for the same child are offset in full. If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top.
- Months in which the mother is entitled to maternity benefits for the same child count as months of basic Elterngeld for her. One day of entitlement in a month is enough for this.
- The offset is by the day. If maternity benefits end partway through a month of the child's life, Elterngeld is paid proportionally for the remaining days. The law says the same: income for only part of a month is offset only against the corresponding part of the Elterngeld.
- The mother's maternity benefits are offset only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

This is the general rule. Whether and by how much it changes your family's payment is decided by the office that handles your Elterngeld application.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, the law allows some paid work. One of the conditions for Elterngeld (parental allowance) is that the person does no paid work or does not work full time (BEEG §1(1) no. 4).

Working changes the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between your earnings before the birth and your earnings in that month. For this calculation, earnings before the birth count up to at most 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

What you state in the application matters. If you said you expected no earnings during the payment period, Elterngeld is paid subject to being withdrawn if you do have earnings. If you said you expected earnings, the amount is decided provisionally, and after the payment period ends you must prove your actual earnings for that time (BEEG §8).

The statute sections provided here do not set a limit in hours. The federal family portal explains that you may work part time while receiving Elterngeld, up to 32 hours a week. That is the portal's summary, not the statute text. The portal also says partly different rules apply for some older births.

Whether your own work meets these conditions, and how much you would receive, is decided only by the Elterngeld office responsible where you live.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: The law says you apply for Kindergeld (child benefit) at the family benefits office responsible for the district where the entitled person lives. That office both receives the application and decides on the claim. If the person has no residence in Germany, the office for their usual place of stay is responsible. Failing that, it is the office for where they work. The Familienportal says this is usually the family benefits office of your local employment agency (Agentur für Arbeit).

How to apply: The law says Kindergeld must be applied for in writing. The Familienportal explains that you can apply electronically or on paper, using the family benefits offices' form. You can fill the form in online, then print and sign it. For a newborn, you can also apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, with no printing or handwritten signature. The application must include your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number.

Who can apply: Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment can apply. Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child. If the child lives in the parents' shared household, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. If they do not decide, the family court decides on application.

Documents: For a child under 18, you normally only need to give the two tax identification numbers. For a child born or living abroad, the Federal Employment Agency asks for a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document certifying the birth. rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
We cover Hessen's state procedures, not Bavaria's, so we cannot tell you how to apply in Bavaria, which office handles it, or which forms it uses. For that, contact the Elterngeld office responsible for where you live in Bavaria. The rules themselves are federal law (BEEG) and apply in Bavaria too. Here is what the excerpts say.

Who can receive it. A person can claim Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they live or usually stay in Germany, live in one household with the child, care for and bring up the child themselves, and do not work, or do not work full time (BEEG §1(1)).

Self-employed income counts. Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. That income includes positive income from farming and forestry, from a trade business, and from self-employed work, where it is taxable in Germany. It is averaged per month over the assessment period set by §2b (BEEG §2(1)). The percentage rises for pre-birth income below 1,000 euros, up to 100 percent. It falls for income above 1,200 euros, down to 65 percent (BEEG §2(2)).

Limits. The maximum is 1,800 euros a month for full months without income from work. The minimum is 300 euros, including for people with no income before the birth (BEEG §2(1) and (4)). If you earn less after the birth than before, Elterngeld is that percentage of the difference. Pre-birth income counts up to 2,770 euros at most for this (BEEG §2(3)).

Provisional decisions and later proof. These rules matter often for self-employed parents. The amount is decided provisionally, based on the information you have made credible, until proof arrives, if any of these applies (BEEG §8(3)):
- the tax assessment for the last completed tax period before the birth is not yet available, and it cannot yet be said whether the amounts in §1(8) are exceeded;
- income before the birth cannot be determined;
- you expect to have income from work during the benefit period.
If your application estimated your income, you must prove your actual income for that time after the benefit period ends (BEEG §8(1)). Payment is made subject to revocation in two cases (BEEG §8(2)):
- you stated you would have no income from work, but you do;
- the tax assessment was not available and you stated the §1(8) amounts would not be exceeded, but they are.

How long. Elterngeld comes in a basic form or a Plus form. One month of the basic form can be taken as two months of the Plus form. The basic form can be received until the child's 14th month of life ends. Parents together have 12 monthly amounts of the basic form. They get 2 more if one parent's income from work is reduced for two months. One parent can have at most 12 basic monthly amounts plus up to 4 partnership-bonus amounts, and must take at least two months (BEEG §4).

What is missing. The excerpts do not contain the provisions on which period self-employed income is measured over (§2b), how it is calculated, or the amounts in §1(8). The Elterngeld office can explain those rules.

Only the responsible Elterngeld office in Bavaria decides whether you qualify and how much you receive.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
We cannot fill in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application for you. The entries on the form are choices and statements about your own family, such as which months you claim and what income you expect. Making those choices for you would be an individual case assessment, which we are not permitted to do. What the law says about the application itself:

- Elterngeld must be applied for in writing. Payment is made retroactively for at most the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.
- The application must state for which months of the child's life you claim each type of payment: the basic allowance, the 'Plus' variant, or the partnership bonus.
- The person applying signs the application. The other entitled parent also signs to confirm they have seen it. Exceptions apply, for example where one person alone has custody. The other parent can at the same time make their own application.
- Choices made in the application can be changed until the end of the payment period. Changes reach back at most three months before the month the change request is received. Months already paid can only be changed in cases of particular hardship. An exception lets you switch a month already paid as 'Plus' to the basic allowance afterwards.
- The official family portal lists the documents usually attached. These include the child's birth certificate and proof of previous income. For employees, that means pay slips for the 12 months before the birth (fathers) or before maternity protection began (mothers). The self-employed usually attach their last tax assessment. Further documents may be needed depending on the case.

The responsible authority is the one your Land designates for the district where the child lives when you first apply. The family portal calls it the parental allowance office. That office decides your application and also gives advice. You can ask it for help with the form.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you how much tax you would save by switching to tax class III. That is a calculation of your own tax, and only a tax adviser or your local tax office can do it.

What the sources do say is how a tax class change before the birth affects parental allowance:

- A tax class change before the birth can change the amount of your taxes and social contributions.
- Parental allowance is calculated from a simplified net income. For this, the most recent tax class counts. The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period.
- The law says the income tax deduction in this calculation is based on your tax class and, where relevant, the factor used with tax class IV. Tax class VI is not taken into account.
- Changing tax class again after the birth has no effect on your parental allowance.

Whether a change would affect your own parental allowance, and by how much, is decided by the office that handles parental allowance applications in your area. Questions about the tax effect of the change belong to a tax adviser or your tax office.
